title: How do you decide the correct number of threads in a thread pool? Explain the formula for CPU-bound work versus IO-bound work, and why oversizing a pool actually hurts performance.
shortTitle: How to size a thread pool?

s1_definition.profdef: Thread pool sizing is the process of choosing how many worker threads a pool should hold so that the CPU stays busy without wasting resources. For CPU-bound work (pure computation), the optimal size is roughly the number of CPU cores plus one, because a thread almost never gives up the core voluntarily. For IO-bound work (waiting on disk, network, or database), the optimal size is cores multiplied by one plus the ratio of wait time to compute time, because threads spend most of their life blocked and the CPU would otherwise sit idle. Oversizing a pool causes excessive context switching, cache thrashing, and higher memory use, which reduces throughput.
s1_definition.analogy: Think of National Bank of India with a fixed number of cash counters (CPU cores). If each teller job is pure counting of notes with no waiting (CPU-bound), then having more tellers than counters is pointless — extra tellers just stand around and bump into each other. But if each teller job involves long phone calls to head office to verify Rajesh's account (IO-bound), then one teller waiting on the phone frees the counter, so you want several tellers per counter so that while one waits on hold, another counts notes. Too many tellers in a small branch, though, and they waste time switching seats and queuing for the same desk.
s1_definition.oneliner: For pure computation use cores plus one; for waiting work use cores times one plus wait-over-compute; never just pick a big round number.
s1_definition.raw:
**Professional definition:** Thread pool sizing is the process of choosing how many worker threads a pool should hold so that the CPU stays busy without wasting resources. For CPU-bound work (pure computation), the optimal size is roughly the number of CPU cores plus one, because a thread almost never gives up the core voluntarily. For IO-bound work (waiting on disk, network, or database), the optimal size is cores multiplied by one plus the ratio of wait time to compute time, because threads spend most of their life blocked and the CPU would otherwise sit idle. Oversizing a pool causes excessive context switching, cache thrashing, and higher memory use, which reduces throughput.

**In simple words (banking analogy):** Think of National Bank of India with a fixed number of cash counters (CPU cores). If each teller job is pure counting of notes with no waiting (CPU-bound), then having more tellers than counters is pointless — extra tellers just stand around and bump into each other. But if each teller job involves long phone calls to head office to verify Rajesh's account (IO-bound), then one teller waiting on the phone frees the counter, so you want several tellers per counter so that while one waits on hold, another counts notes. Too many tellers in a small branch, though, and they waste time switching seats and queuing for the same desk.

**One line to remember:** For pure computation use cores plus one; for waiting work use cores times one plus wait-over-compute; never just pick a big round number.

sections.s2_technical:
The core idea is that a CPU core can only run one thread at a time. If your task never blocks — it just crunches numbers like calculating interest on a million accounts — then adding more threads than cores does not give you more parallelism. The extra threads simply wait their turn and the operating system wastes time swapping them on and off the core. That swapping is called a context switch, and each one costs CPU cycles to save and restore registers and pollutes the CPU cache.

For CPU-bound work the classic formula is `numberOfThreads = numberOfCores + 1`. The plus one exists so that if one thread is briefly paused by a page fault, another is ready to keep the core busy. You read the core count at runtime with `Runtime.getRuntime().availableProcessors()`. For example, on an 8-core server you would create `Executors.newFixedThreadPool(9)` for a heavy portfolio risk calculation.

For IO-bound work the formula is `numberOfThreads = numberOfCores * (1 + waitTime / computeTime)`. Here waitTime is how long a task spends blocked (waiting for the database to return Rajesh's balance) and computeTime is how long it actually uses the CPU. If a task waits 90 milliseconds and computes for 10 milliseconds, the ratio is 9, so on 8 cores you want `8 * (1 + 9) = 80` threads. The reasoning is that while 9 threads are blocked on IO, 1 can use the core, so you need roughly 10 threads per core to keep every core busy.

A senior nuance is that these formulas are starting points, not final answers. The only reliable method is to measure. You set a size, run a realistic load test, watch CPU utilization and throughput, and adjust. You also must bound the queue. A common production bug is using an unbounded `LinkedBlockingQueue` which hides the fact that your pool is too small — tasks pile up in memory until the server runs out of heap. A bounded queue plus a sensible `RejectedExecutionHandler` (like `CallerRunsPolicy`) applies natural back-pressure.

```java
int cores = Runtime.getRuntime().availableProcessors();
int cpuBound = cores + 1;                       // interest computation
int ioBound  = cores * (1 + (90 / 10));          // DB-heavy work, wait/compute = 9
ThreadPoolExecutor pool = new ThreadPoolExecutor(
        ioBound, ioBound, 60L, java.util.concurrent.TimeUnit.SECONDS,
        new java.util.concurrent.ArrayBlockingQueue<>(500),      // bounded!
        new java.util.concurrent.ThreadPoolExecutor.CallerRunsPolicy());
```

Oversizing hurts for three concrete reasons. First, context switching: with 500 threads on 8 cores the OS constantly swaps threads, and those switches can consume a measurable slice of CPU that should have gone to real work. Second, memory: each thread reserves a stack (often one megabyte), so 500 threads reserve roughly 500 megabytes just for stacks. Third, cache locality: each thread has its own working set, and constant switching evicts useful data from the CPU cache, so every thread runs slower after it resumes.
sections.s3_banking:
National Bank of India runs two very different nightly jobs, and the operations team keeps getting the thread count wrong.

Problem 1 — The interest calculation job. Every night the bank computes compound interest on Rajesh's savings account SAV2001 and millions of others. This is pure math — no database calls inside the loop, the data is already loaded in memory. A junior engineer set the pool to 200 threads thinking "more threads, more speed," but the 8-core server actually got slower because 200 threads fought over 8 cores and the machine spent its time context switching. This is exactly how CPU-bound sizing works — the right size is cores plus one, because a computing thread never yields the core voluntarily.

Problem 2 — The statement generation job. The bank also generates PDF statements, and each statement requires several slow calls: fetch Priya's transactions for CUR3001 from the database, call a remote formatting service, and write a file. Each task waits far longer than it computes. The same engineer used cores plus one here too, and the job crawled because 9 threads spent 90 percent of their time blocked while 8 cores sat idle. This is exactly how IO-bound sizing works — you need many threads per core so that some can compute while most wait.

The mini-project builds a `ThreadPoolSizer` helper that computes the recommended size for each workload type, a `CpuBoundTask` (interest math) and an `IoBoundTask` (simulated database wait), and a demo that runs both with the wrong and right sizes to show the throughput difference. The test asserts that the computed sizes match the formulas and that the IO-bound size is much larger than the CPU-bound size.

sections.s5_journey:
Input: an 8-core server, an IO task that waits 90 milliseconds and computes 10 milliseconds, and a CPU task that computes compound interest for Rajesh.

**Step 1.** The sizer reads cores = 8. For the CPU-bound interest job it returns 8 + 1 = 9. The data here is just an integer recommendation; nothing is executed yet.

**Step 2.** For the IO-bound statement job the sizer plugs wait = 90 and compute = 10 into cores times one plus wait over compute: 8 times 10 equals 80. So it recommends 80 threads. The ratio 9 tells us each task is blocked 90 percent of the time.

**Step 3.** The CPU task runs its tight multiplication loop 100000 times with no blocking. One thread fully occupies one core the whole time, so adding more threads than 9 would only add context switching.

**Step 4.** The IO task calls `Thread.sleep(90)`, which releases the core. During those 90 milliseconds the pool can run 9 other IO tasks on the same core, which is why 80 threads keep all 8 cores busy.

**Step 5.** The final output prints the two recommended sizes and the computed results, confirming the IO size (80) is far larger than the CPU size (9).

```
INFO  CPU-bound size on 8 cores = 9
INFO  IO-bound size on 8 cores (wait=90ms compute=10ms) = 80
INFO  Recommended CPU-bound pool: 9
INFO  Recommended IO-bound pool:  80
INFO  Rajesh SAV2001 interest result: 1051270.94
INFO  Priya CUR3001 statement result: STATEMENT-CUR3001
```
sections.s5b_flow:
```
  Input: 8 cores, IO task wait=90ms compute=10ms, CPU interest task
    │
    ▼
  ThreadPoolSizer(cores=8)
    │
    ├─ CPU-BOUND PATH                   ├─ IO-BOUND PATH
    │  size = cores + 1                 │  ratio = wait/compute = 90/10 = 9
    │  size = 8 + 1 = 9                 │  size = cores × (1 + ratio)
    │  reason: thread never yields core │  size = 8 × (1 + 9) = 80
    ▼                                   ▼
  9 threads on 8 cores                 80 threads on 8 cores
  (1 spare for page faults)            (9 wait while 1 computes per core)
    │                                   │
    ▼                                   ▼
  CpuBoundTask.call()                  IoBoundTask.call()
  tight loop, core 100% busy           Thread.sleep(90) → core FREE
    │                                   │
    ▼                                   ▼
  result: Rs.1,051,270.94              result: STATEMENT-CUR3001

  OVERSIZE WARNING:
  200 threads on 8 cores → constant context switching → SLOWER
  200 × 1MB stack = 200MB wasted memory
```

sections.s6_takeaway:
Thread pool sizing depends entirely on whether the work is CPU-bound or IO-bound, and the biggest mistake teams make is picking a large round number and hoping for the best. For CPU-bound work such as computing compound interest or risk scores, the right size is the number of cores plus one, because a thread that is purely computing never gives up its core voluntarily, so any threads beyond the core count simply wait and force the operating system into wasteful context switching. The plus one covers the brief moments when a thread is paused by a page fault.

For IO-bound work such as generating statements, where each task spends most of its life waiting on the database or a remote service, the right size is the number of cores multiplied by one plus the ratio of wait time to compute time. In a real project at National Bank of India we measured that each statement task waited about 90 milliseconds and computed for about 10 milliseconds, giving a ratio of nine, so on an eight-core box we ran roughly 80 threads. The reasoning is that while nine threads are blocked on IO, one can keep the core busy, so you need about ten threads per core.

I always stress that these formulas are starting points, not final answers. The only reliable approach is to set a size, run a realistic load test, watch CPU utilization and throughput, and adjust from there. I also always bound the queue with an ArrayBlockingQueue and configure a rejection policy such as CallerRunsPolicy, because an unbounded queue hides an undersized pool and lets tasks pile up until the server runs out of heap.

Finally, I explain why oversizing actively hurts rather than just wasting resources. Too many threads cause constant context switching that burns CPU cycles meant for real work, each thread reserves about a megabyte of stack so hundreds of threads waste hundreds of megabytes, and the constant switching evicts useful data from the CPU cache so every thread runs slower after it resumes. In short, the correct size keeps every core busy with the fewest threads possible, and the only way to confirm it is to measure under real load.

---

keyPoints: Always benchmark — formulas are starting points
